question.:question/problem: What is the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=18 x - 45 \cos{\left(x \right)}$ at the point $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$?
question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope is the derivative evaluated at $x=\frac{\pi}{6}.$

We know that $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sin x)=\cos x,$ and that $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\cos x)=-\sin x.$ Applying these formulas and the sum and constant multiple rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} &= \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(18 x - 45 \cos{\left(x \right)}) \\ &= (45 \sin{\left(x \right)})+(18) \\ &= 45 \sin{\left(x \right)} + 18.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi}{6},$ we get

$$
y^{\prime}(\frac{\pi}{6})=18+45\sin(\frac{\pi}{6})=18+45\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{81}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the slope is $\frac{81}{2}.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If we let $u=18 x + \frac{\pi}{3},$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=18\,\Longrightarrow\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{18}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Calculating the limits for $u$ gives

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{54}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{2 \pi}{3}$ |

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{54}}\sin{\left(18 x + \frac{\pi}{3} \right)}\,\text{d}x &= {\int }_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}1\sin(u)\cdot \frac{1}{18}\,\text{d}u \\ &= \frac{1}{18}{\int }_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}}\sin(u)\,\text{d}u \\ &= - \frac{\cos{\left(u \right)}}{18}\big|_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{2 \pi}{3}} \\ &= \frac{1}{36}-(- \frac{1}{36}) \\ &= \frac{1}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{\sin x}{13x}$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=\pi$.

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}(x)&=\frac{u^{\prime}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot v^{\prime}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}}\\ &=\frac{(\sin{\left(x \right)})^{\prime}\cdot (13 x)-(\sin{\left(x \right)})\cdot (13 x)^{\prime}}{(13 x)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{(\cos{\left(x \right)})\cdot (13 x)-(\sin{\left(x \right)})\cdot (13)}{(13 x)^{2}}\\ &=\frac{13 \left(x \cos{\left(x \right)} - \sin{\left(x \right)}\right)}{169 x^{2}}\\ &=\frac{x \cos{\left(x \right)} - \sin{\left(x \right)}}{13 x^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=\pi$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}f^{\prime}(\pi)&=\frac{\pi\cos(\pi)-\sin(\pi)}{13\pi^{2}}\\ &=\frac{\pi(-1)-0}{13\pi^{2}}\\ &=- \frac{1}{13 \pi}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $- \frac{1}{13 \pi}.$

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=x y e^{x y} + e^{x y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x^{2} e^{x y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =3 t^{7} e^{3 t^{7}} + e^{3 t^{7}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =9 t^{8} e^{3 t^{7}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &=12 t^{3},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=3 t^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =(3 t^{7} e^{3 t^{7}} + e^{3 t^{7}})\cdot (12 t^{3})+(9 t^{8} e^{3 t^{7}})\cdot (3 t^{2}) \\  & =12 t^{3} e^{3 t^{7}} + (36 t^{10} e^{3 t^{7}}) + (27 t^{10} e^{3 t^{7}}) \\  & =3 t^{3} (21 t^{7} + 4) e^{3 t^{7}}.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable

question.:question/problem: If $f(x,y)=x e^{x y},$ $x=(t + 3)^{3}$ and $y=(t + 3)^{2},$ compute $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/f0/f01b253f560405a8c0f4be8f8797c652fb0ddf774f4db110b8822313b8ac50f3.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x=x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} &=x y e^{x y} + e^{x y},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=x^{2} e^{x y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =(t + 3)^{5} e^{(t + 3)^{5}} + e^{(t + 3)^{5}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =(t + 3)^{6} e^{(t + 3)^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} &=3 (t + 3)^{2},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}=2 t + 6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} \\  & =((t + 3)^{5} e^{(t + 3)^{5}} + e^{(t + 3)^{5}})\cdot (3 (t + 3)^{2})+((t + 3)^{6} e^{(t + 3)^{5}})\cdot (2 t + 6) \\  & =3 (t + 3)^{2} e^{(t + 3)^{5}} + (3 (t + 3)^{7} e^{(t + 3)^{5}}) + ((t + 3)^{6} (2 t + 6) e^{(t + 3)^{5}}) \\  & =(t + 3)^{2} (5 (t + 3)^{5} + 3) e^{(t + 3)^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$
